analysis.one_liner: Bans bisphenol A (BPA) in food and beverage containers and tightens FDA review of chemicals deemed safe in food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban BPA in food containers was never taken up by the Senate committee it was referred to and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to sell food or beverages in containers made with or releasing bisphenol A, a chemical used in many hard plastics and can linings that researchers have linked to hormone-related health effects. It also would have required the FDA to periodically re-review chemicals on its 'generally recognized as safe' list and to restrict any that new science shows can cause reproductive or developmental harm, with temporary waivers and warning labels where BPA could not yet be replaced. The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially pregnant women, infants, and young children, would gain the most, since BPA in food packaging is a pervasive exposure route and the bill targeted it at the source rather than relying on consumer avoidance. The bill would also benefit states and tribes by expressly preserving their right to set stricter rules than the federal standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially pregnant women and infants

how_it_helps.text: Bans any food or beverage container composed of, or able to release, bisphenol A into food, treating it as a poisonous or deleterious substance under federal food law.
Requires FDA to periodically review substances on the 'generally recognized as safe' list and to ban or restrict any that new scientific evidence shows cause reproductive or developmental toxicity.
Requires food-contact substance manufacturers to notify FDA of health-effect determinations, including low-dose exposure and reproductive toxicity, rather than leaving that notification optional.

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage companies using BPA-based cans, jars, and plastics would bear the cost of switching to alternatives, and chemical makers selling BPA would lose that market. Some costs would likely be passed on to consumers through prices in the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food packaging companies and BPA makers

drawbacks.text: The Secretary could grant one-year, renewable waivers to facilities that could not yet replace BPA, meaning some products could still reach store shelves in BPA containers for up to two years—labeled with a warning.
Mandating a fast industry-wide switch from BPA would impose replacement costs on food and beverage companies and could raise packaging costs for consumers in the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—removing a suspected endocrine disruptor from baby bottles, canned food, and infant formula packaging—was real and would have been achievable, since industry was already phasing out BPA in some products and the bill built in waivers and phase-in time for products where replacement was hard. The costs are modest: higher packaging costs passed through to consumers, and some loss of packaging performance until substitutes prove out. On balance a public-health gain, though the bill never advanced far enough for its design flaws (waiver duration, preemption questions, testing feasibility) to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and no action was ever taken on it, so it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on March 12, 2009, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll-call votes in either chamber.
The bill expired with the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011, and BPA remained legal in food containers at the federal level.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food, beverage, and packaging manufacturers that relied on BPA benefited because the ban never took effect, and consumers were left without the federal protection the bill would have provided.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action—hearing, markup, or report—on it.

against.name: Chemical and packaging industry interests
against.what_they_did: Ran a well-documented public campaign defending the safety of BPA and opposing state and federal restrictions on its use.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all known support came from Democrats, but the bill never advanced far enough to reveal whether opposition was partisan.

industries.industry: Food and beverage canning and packaging companies
industries.note: The bill would ban BPA-based containers after 180 days and force a switch to alternatives, with limited waivers available where replacement was not technologically feasible. Consumers would face no direct new cost beyond possible price effects from packaging changes.

The primary food-market buyer of BPA—food containers—would be closed off by statute, cutting demand. Meanwhile the bill allows states to impose stricter rules, limiting any rollback of local protections.

The bill makes safety notification to FDA mandatory rather than optional and subjects the GRAS list to periodic review with mandatory remedial action, tightening oversight of an industry that previously faced a largely voluntary process.
